newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: RATE CUT NO PANACEA FOR CZECH ECONOMY - ECONOMISTS.
newsitem.headline: RATE CUT NO PANACEA FOR CZECH ECONOMY - ECONOMISTS.

text.p: The Czech economy, once praised as the flagship of post-communist reform, is heading into a sharp economic downturn and only a weaker crown and radical company restructuring can pull it back up, economists say.

In the first three months of the year, official figures showed real industrial output falling 4.2 percent compared with the first quarter of 1996 while construction output fell 5.2 percent in the same period.

"I think it is now quite possible that GDP (gross domestic product) will have no growth in the first quarter of this year," Vladimir Kreidl of Patria Finance told Reuters. First quarter GDP data is scheduled to be released on June 19.
The government fiercely rejects any talk of a crisis, and the central bank is adamant there will be no devaluation of the crown.

But Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus does acknowledge there will be almost no growth in the economy this quarter and he has admitted that full year GDP growth of 2.7 percent, half the government's original 1997 forecast, would be a "success"..
In response to the downturn, the government introduced a package of measures to boost growth and support exports.
Government officials have also lambasted the central bank for its tight monetary policy and are calling for a cut in interest rates.
The discount rate was raised last summer to 10.5 percent from 9.5. as part of a series of tightening moves to choke off inflationary pressure brought about by a growing money supply.
However, economists argue that an easing would do little to attack the real problem -- a lack of economic restructuring.

"Restructuring in many parts of the Czech economy has not proceded as far as it should have and the fact that the central bank tightened its policy only revealed these problems sooner than they would otherwise have been revealed," said Kreidl.
"The primary reason is the micro-level and not the policy of the central bank," he added.

Along with falling output, the Czech economy has been plagued by a massive and growing current account deficit which rose to 8.6 percent of gross domestic product in 1996 from around three percent in 1995 and just 0.1 percent in 1994.

Kreidl said part of the solution to both problems may be a crown devaluation which could provide for a period of non-inflationary, export-led growth, boosting the economy and reining in the current account deficit at the same time.

He rejected a cut in interest rates as the best solution, saying the effects would be too general and risked promoting the kind of consumer led boom which was largely responsible for the massive inflow of imports in the first place.
The crown has been weakening steadily in recent weeks but the central bank has said it would defend the currency if it fell much further.

On Wednesday, it was trading at around 3.5 percent below its dollar/mark basket parity, a nine percentage point swing from the beginning of February when it hit a record 5.51 percent on the appreciation side of the basket midpoint.
"I think that starting from May this year there will be new opportunities for Czech exporters (owing to) the lowering of the crown rate," said Pavel Sobisek of Zivnostenska Banka.

The downturn in the economy in 1997 has been reflected in poor first quarter earnings from many of the country's biggest companies, leading many economists to believe that corporate restructuring is also at the heart of the problem.
Rob van de Wijngaert, an economist at ABN AMRO Hoare Govett, said the weakness of the micro-economy could also be discerned from the structural dynamics of the current account deficit itself.

"Czech firms are a bit sluggish in implementing their capital inputs. They're heavily importing machinery and other tools but at the same time we don't see a pick up in exports... It's the long lag time that worries me," he said.
Government officials and private economists alike have long said that the current account deficit was less significant than it appeared.

They argue that a deficit is natural for an emerging economy that needs to import heavily to re-tool and bring efficiency to Communist-era factories, subsequently allowing for a surge in exports when restructuring has been completed.

A rush to import machinery pushed the trade deficit to a record 160.2 billion crowns for 1996 -- the central bank estimates that investment goods account for 37 percent of total imports -- and is headed towards 200 billion crowns this year.
Van de Wijngaert said he was also concerned that the failure of company management to produce high quality goods efficiently was reflected in the direction of Czech exports.

"Also the share of exports to developed market economies is falling. There was about 67 percent export share to developed economies in the last two quarters of 1995 whereas in the last two quarters of 1996 that has fallen to 63.3," he said.
